pairs.rationale: The question asks what advantage belongs to the Jew and circumcision. The later discussion lists Israelite adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises, fathers and the Christ according to flesh. That list supplies a fuller privilege discussion, not a claim that these advantages exempt anyone from the sin charge developed here.

Romans names being entrusted with God’s oracles as the advantage. Stephen describes Moses receiving living oracles to give to his people in the wilderness. The shared received revelation connects the statements, while the recipients, Sinai setting and singular mediator are not identical formulations.

Romans asks whether some people’s unfaithfulness nullifies God’s faithfulness; the letter says that if we are unfaithful He remains faithful. The shared contrast does not erase the adjacent letter’s warning about denying Him or turn either statement into an unqualified verdict on every individual’s outcome.

The quoted justification-in-God’s-words and prevailing-when-judged language corresponds to this psalm’s confession of sin before God. Romans applies it while insisting on God’s truth against human falsehood. The psalm’s personal confession and the letter’s argument remain distinct, with the actual quotation forms retained.

Romans’s every-human-being-a-liar formula has a close counterpart in the psalm’s every-man-a-liar statement. The psalm attributes its statement to the speaker’s bewilderment; Romans contrasts human falsehood with God’s truth. That framing is not silently transferred between the passages.

Both passages frame a question about unrighteousness with God and reject it. Romans3 raises wrath and explicitly marks human terms; Romans9 raises the question amid the Jacob/Esau and mercy discussion. These are presented objections, not assertions that God is unrighteous.

Paul’s rejection appeals to God judging the world. Abraham likewise appeals to the One judging all the earth doing justice, while pleading against sweeping righteous and ungodly away together. The shared justice premise is used in different arguments, without making the Sodom plea a quotation of Paul’s objection.

The question about personal falsehood advancing divine truth parallels the earlier question about human unrighteousness displaying God’s righteousness. The earlier objection is rejected with an appeal to divine judgment. This identifies the argumentative pattern without treating the question as a confession that Paul lied for God’s glory.

Here Paul condemns the slandered proposal to do evil so good may come. Later he asks whether remaining in sin could increase grace and emphatically rejects it. The proposed benefits differ, but both passages refuse turning a claimed divine good into permission to continue wrongdoing.

Romans charges Jews and Greeks alike with being under sin. Galatians describes Scripture confining everything under sin so that the faith-in-Jesus promise is given to believers. The universal sin language corresponds, while the confinement image and stated promise purpose are the letter’s additional formulation.

Romans opens its Scripture chain with no righteous one, not even one. Ecclesiastes says no righteous person on earth does good without sinning. The shared universal righteousness-and-sin claim has different wording; the link does not identify Ecclesiastes as an indisputable verbatim source of the chain’s opening line.

The psalm describes the Lord’s search for anyone understanding or seeking God, followed by everyone turning aside. Romans gives the negative understanding-and-seeking conclusion within its chain. The psalm’s searching question and ensuing answer are preserved rather than presented as exactly the same sentence.

The all-turned-aside, together-useless and no-kindness-not-one lines closely match the beginning of this saved psalm unit. That original unit continues with additional throat-to-no-fear lines as well; they are not excised or divided into manufactured verse IDs.

The opened-tomb throat and tongues practicing deceit clauses correspond to the psalm’s throat and tongue description. The psalm also speaks about mouth and heart, which Romans does not repeat in these clauses. The separate asp-poison clause is not assigned to this target.

The asp poison beneath the lips corresponds to this psalm’s asp venom beneath their lips. The target also compares sharpened tongues with a serpent. The shared lip-and-asp image is precise, while poison/venom rendering and the additional tongue line remain as saved.

Both lines describe a mouth full of cursing and bitterness. The psalm uses his mouth and also includes deceit; Romans uses their mouth and omits that third item here. The quotation correspondence does not erase those pronoun and list differences.

Romans’s feet swift to pour out blood corresponds to Isaiah’s feet running toward wickedness and quick to shed blood. The bloodshed image is shared, while the extra wickedness and foolish-thought clauses are not inserted into Paul’s shorter line.

The ruin-and-misery-in-their-ways line corresponds to Isaiah’s destruction and misery in their ways. Isaiah places it with feet running to wrongdoing and foolish thoughts. Romans retains its shorter chain clause rather than reproducing every surrounding charge.

Both passages speak of not knowing the way of peace. Isaiah adds the absence of justice and twisted paths, and uses its own present wording; Romans gives the shorter past-worded clause. Those additional accusations and formulations are not silently merged.

The no-fear-of-God-before-the-eyes statement corresponds to the psalm’s description of the lawless person. The psalm has his eyes, while Romans has their eyes within its collective chain. The singular lawless-person setting and his/their pronoun difference remain distinct.

Romans3 makes the whole world answerable to God as mouths are stopped. The later admonition says all the addressed community will stand before God’s judgment seat and each give account. The accountability corresponds, with world-versus-community scope and different immediate arguments retained.

Both passages deny justification by works of law, explicitly extending the denial to no flesh. Galatians also states faith in Jesus Christ; Romans adds that law brings knowledge of sin. Neither passage’s additional explanation is silently substituted for the other.

Romans says God’s revealed righteousness is witnessed by law and prophets even while describing it as apart from law. Jesus names the Law of Moses, Prophets and Psalms as writings about Him that must be fulfilled. The Scripture-witness connection does not make Luke repeat Paul’s apart-from-law formula or remove either role given to law here.

Romans connects righteousness with faith in Jesus Christ for all believers and no distinction. Galatians connects sonship with faith in Christ Jesus and says Jew and Greek and its additional categories are one in Him. The inclusion theme corresponds without treating righteousness and sonship as identical words or adding every Galatian category to this verse.

Romans concludes that all sinned and fall short of God’s glory. Solomon’s prayer introduces possible sin and captivity with the acknowledgment that no person will not sin. The human sin claim corresponds, while the glory language and the prayer’s possible captivity scenario are not transferred between statements.

Romans describes free justification by grace through redemption in Christ Jesus. Ephesians likewise speaks of redemption through His blood and forgiveness according to rich grace. The grace-and-redemption connection preserves justification versus forgiveness wording rather than making every clause a verbatim restatement.

Romans describes God setting Christ forth as propitiation in His blood through faith and discusses passing over earlier sins. The letter explicitly names Jesus Christ as advocate and propitiation for sins. The shared propitiation language does not make that target repeat every blood, faith or earlier-sins clause.

Romans joins God’s righteousness with justifying the one having faith in Jesus. The letter calls Him faithful and just to forgive and cleanse confessed sins. The divine justice and saving-action connection preserves the distinct faith/confession conditions and justification/forgiveness words instead of replacing one formulation with the other.

Romans excludes boasting through a law of faith rather than works. Ephesians describes salvation by grace through faith as God’s gift, not from works so that no one boasts. The exclusion corresponds, without making Ephesians repeat the law-of-faith expression.

Romans reckons a person justified by faith apart from works of law; James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The comparison preserves works of law versus works and their different argument settings. It does not insert alone into Romans or supply an unreported explanation making the two statements verbatim equivalents.

Paul affirms that God is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews. Peter’s speech rejects divine partiality and accepts those fearing God and practicing righteousness in every nation. The national inclusion corresponds, while Peter’s stated response language and Paul’s faith-justification argument are not collapsed into one quotation.

Paul’s one-God premise accompanies justification of circumcised from faith and uncircumcised through faith. Deuteronomy’s address to Israel declares the Lord our God one. The monotheistic statement connects, but the faith clauses and their different prepositions are Paul’s formulation, not an added Deuteronomic line.

Paul rejects nullifying law through faith and speaks of establishing it. Jesus rejects coming to abolish Law or Prophets and speaks of fulfillment. The rejection of abolition connects, while establishing and fulfilling remain different words and neither passage is turned into an unquoted rule resolving every later law question.

The opening asks what Abraham has found; the ensuing argument explicitly turns to Scripture’s faith-and-righteousness statement about him. This identifies the proof text to which the question leads, not an independent account of his ancestry or every step of the works-and-boasting discussion.

Romans argues conditionally that works-based justification would give Abraham a boast, but not before God. James affirms justification in the Isaac-offering episode and describes faith working with works and brought to completion. The different arguments and use of the same righteousness Scripture remain visible, without adding an unstated before-humans versus before-God scheme.

The belief-in-God and reckoned-as-righteousness statement closely matches Genesis. Genesis here names Abram, whereas Romans uses Abraham. The later name form and the surrounding promise argument are retained without rewriting the earlier narrative’s actual name.

The wage illustration distinguishes what is owed to a worker from grace. The later remnant discussion likewise contrasts grace with works so that grace remains grace. The logical contrast connects distinct topics; the remnant statement is not another employment illustration or a claim that every wage is salvation.

Here the One justifies the ungodly and reckons the believer’s faith as righteousness. The later explanation describes Christ dying for the ungodly while they were weak. The undeserving recipients and saving provision connect, while death and faith-reckoning are distinct formulations rather than one repeated sentence.

Paul introduces David’s blessedness statement about reckoning righteousness apart from works. The saved psalm names David and pronounces forgiveness, covered sins and non-reckoning of sin. Paul’s righteousness-apart-from-works framing interprets those lines rather than pretending the psalm states every part of that introduction verbatim.

Both texts call blessed those whose lawless deeds are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Romans gives its own tense formulation within the argument. The psalm’s David-and-understanding heading remains original context and is not appended to the Pauline quotation.

The blessed man whose sin the Lord will certainly not reckon corresponds closely to this psalm line. The psalm additionally describes no deceit in his mouth; Romans does not include that additional clause in this quotation.

The circumcision question is supported by repeating that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. Genesis narrates Abram believing God and the reckoning. The circumcised-versus-uncircumcised question is Paul’s application, not a question stated in that earlier verse.

Paul asks when righteousness was reckoned and answers before circumcision. Genesis15 supplies the earlier belief-and-reckoning event. That selected verse does not itself say uncircumcised; the later covenant-sign instructions provide the other part of Paul’s narrative-order argument.

The circumcision instructions and sign description occur later in Genesis than the belief-and-reckoning notice in15:6. This supplies the second event used by Paul’s before-circumcision argument, without manufacturing an exact elapsed interval or claiming these instructions repeat the earlier reckoning.

Genesis calls circumcision a sign of the covenant. Paul calls the received sign a seal of the righteousness of Abraham’s earlier faith and draws a fatherhood conclusion. The shared sign connects, while the seal, faith chronology and father-of-believers interpretation are not inserted into Genesis’s actual wording.

Romans describes circumcised people walking in Abraham’s prior faith rather than relying only on circumcision. Galatians calls people of faith Abraham’s sons and blesses them with believing Abraham. The faith-family relation corresponds, while the circumcision qualification and footstep image remain specific to Romans.

Both discussions connect Abraham, his seed, promise and inheritance while denying law as its basis. Galatians specifies Christ as seed and the later law’s430-year interval; Romans uses heir-of-the-world and righteousness-of-faith wording. Those different arguments and details are not transferred between passages.

Romans argues that making law the basis of heirship empties faith and nullifies promise. Galatians likewise says inheritance from law would no longer be from promise, whereas God granted it to Abraham through promise. The related contrast retains each argument’s actual faith and gift wording.

The law-wrath and no-law/no-transgression statement is followed later by sin existing before law but not being charged when no law exists. The relation to law connects, while sin, transgression and charging are not silently made identical or expanded into a claim that no wrongdoing exists apart from law.

Romans grounds the secure promise for all the seed in faith and grace, including both groups it names. Galatians describes those belonging to Christ as Abraham’s seed and heirs according to promise. The inclusive heirship connects without replacing Romans’s law-and-faith distinctions with an unquoted formulation.

The father-of-many-nations statement quotes the promise accompanying Abram’s change of name to Abraham. Romans adds its description of the God he trusted as giving life and calling what is not. Those added divine-ability clauses are not claimed to occur in this Genesis verse.

The so-shall-your-seed-be words recall the Lord taking Abram outside to consider the stars. Paul places the promise in an against-hope belief argument and many-nations conclusion. Genesis’s star image supplies the quoted setting without making every Pauline explanatory phrase part of the original speech.

Romans has Abraham consider his deadened body at about100 and Sarah’s womb without weakening in faith. Genesis records his hundred-year and Sarah’s ninety-year questions together with laughter. The shared age-and-parenthood setting retains the different response descriptions, without changing considered to did-not-consider or explaining the laughter’s unreported motive.

Romans describes Abraham strengthened in faith and giving glory to God over the promise. Hebrews describes Sarah beyond childbearing age receiving conception power because she considered the Promiser faithful. The family promise and faith correspond, while Sarah and Abraham and their particular response descriptions remain distinct.

Romans describes assurance that God can do what He promised. Hebrews has Abraham reason that God can even raise the dead in the Isaac-offering episode and calls the return figurative. The trust in divine ability corresponds across different episodes, without claiming that Isaac actually died or was bodily resurrected.

The therefore-reckoned-as-righteousness conclusion resumes the earlier cited belief-and-reckoning statement in Genesis. The narrative’s Abram name and original context are retained, while Paul draws his own conclusion from the preceding faith discussion.

Paul says the reckoning statement was not written for Abraham alone. The later general statement says earlier writings were for the readers’ instruction, perseverance, encouragement and hope. The application to later readers connects, without claiming every ancient text is the same sentence or was unrelated to its original recipient.

Romans applies the reckoning to believers in the One who raised Jesus our Lord. The letter similarly describes believers in God through Christ, God raising Him and giving Him glory. The God-directed faith and resurrection connect; the letter does not repeat the reckoned-righteousness wording.

Romans joins Jesus’ being handed over for trespasses and raised for justification. The Corinthian gospel summary likewise has Christ die for sins, be buried and be raised. Its third-day and according-to-Scripture details and Romans’s explicit justification purpose remain their separate formulations.
